title: Managing a Small Business in Australia: The Complete Handbook
author: John W. English and Babette Moate
summary:
Managing a Small Business in Australia is a practical, reference-style handbook by John English and Babette Moate aimed at Australian small business owners and aspiring entrepreneurs, structured around the full lifecycle of building and running a business — from initial decision through daily operations to financial management. English, an academic in entrepreneurship and the author of the earlier bestselling How to Organise and Operate a Small Business in Australia, and Moate, his frequent co-author, wrote this as an updated, expanded successor aimed at both people getting started and people already running a business who want to sharpen their operation.

The book opens by acknowledging that small business owners are, in the authors' words, often "the rebels of the business world" — people driven by independence and a desire to put their own ideas into practice, but who don't always come equipped with the practical skills a business actually requires to survive. Part A works through the earliest decisions: the different pathways into starting a business (buying an existing business, starting from scratch, or buying a franchise), how to think through business strategy at the outset, and the baseline legal obligations an Australian small business owner needs to understand from day one, including checking for existing liabilities when buying an established business.

Part B is a distinctly Australian-context section covering where new business owners can actually go for help — government assistance programs and private-sector advisory resources — treating this as practical, not optional, information given how much support exists but goes unused because owners don't know where to look. Part C moves into marketing, covering how to build a marketing strategy, generate sales, and, for businesses ready to scale beyond the domestic market, the basics of export marketing.

Part D addresses operations: choosing and establishing business premises, building an effective day-to-day operating strategy, and the practicalities of employing staff, including obligations that come with taking on employees in the Australian regulatory context. Part E closes the book with financial management — reading and using financial information, managing working capital, sourcing finance, and understanding taxation obligations — closing with the authors' pointed reminder that a business can, counterintuitively, "go broke making a profit" if cash flow isn't managed carefully.

The book's strength is its comprehensiveness and its specifically Australian regulatory and institutional focus, which distinguishes it from the many small-business books written for a US or generic audience. Its limitation is one inherent to any hands-on regulatory handbook: specific legal, tax, and government-assistance details date quickly, and a reader relying on this book years after its edition date should verify current rules rather than treating the book's specifics as up to date.

sections.title: Getting Started (Part A: Pathways to a Start-Up / Business Strategy / Legal Obligations)
sections.summary:
This opening part sets out to walk a prospective business owner through the earliest, highest-stakes decisions: how to actually enter business ownership, and what legal groundwork needs to be in place before trading begins. It covers the different pathways into ownership — starting a business from nothing, buying an existing business, or buying into a franchise — with practical guidance on evaluating each, including due diligence steps like checking for existing liabilities, mortgages, or back taxes attached to a business being purchased.

The middle of the part covers basic business strategy formulation at the outset — clarifying what the business will actually do, for whom, and how it will differentiate itself — before moving into the legal obligations a new Australian small business owner needs to understand from the start, including business structure choices and registration requirements.

The part hands off to Part B by acknowledging that new owners rarely have to figure all of this out alone — substantial help exists, which the book turns to next.
keyLessons: Buying an existing business requires specific due diligence (liabilities, mortgages, back taxes) that a from-scratch startup doesn't.
Business strategy should be clarified before legal structure and operational decisions are finalized, not worked out reactively afterward.
Understanding basic legal obligations from day one prevents costly problems later in the business's life.

sections.title: Getting Help (Part B: Government Assistance / Private Sector Assistance)
sections.summary:
This part sets out to correct a common gap in small business books written for other markets: it treats Australian government and private-sector support resources as a core, practical part of running a small business, not an afterthought. It covers what kinds of government assistance programs exist for small business owners in Australia, and how to access and evaluate private-sector advisory and support services (accountants, business advisors, industry associations).

The substance is oriented toward making sure readers don't leave available support unused simply because they don't know it exists or don't know how to navigate access to it, treating this as a genuine competitive disadvantage for owners who go it entirely alone.

The part hands off to Part C by noting that once a business has its foundational support in place, attention turns to actually generating revenue, which the book takes up next.
keyLessons: Significant government assistance for Australian small businesses often goes unused simply because owners don't know it exists.
Private-sector advisory resources (accountants, industry associations) are treated as a practical necessity, not an optional expense.

sections.title: Marketing Plan (Part C: Marketing Strategy / Generating Sales / Export Marketing)
sections.summary:
This part sets out the commercial engine of the business: how to build a marketing strategy, translate that strategy into actual sales, and, for businesses ready to grow beyond the domestic market, how to approach export marketing. It covers the basics of positioning, identifying target customers, and building a sales process that consistently converts marketing effort into revenue.

The chapter on export marketing extends the book's scope beyond a purely domestic small-business audience, covering the additional considerations (market research, logistics, regulatory differences) that come with selling into international markets.

The part hands off to Part D by noting that marketing and sales success creates operational demands the business needs to be structurally ready to handle.
keyLessons: Marketing strategy and the ability to generate actual sales are treated as distinct, sequential skills, not the same thing.
Export marketing requires additional research and planning beyond domestic marketing strategy.

sections.title: Operations Plan (Part D: Establishing Premises / Operating Strategy / Employing Staff)
sections.summary:
This part sets out the practical, physical, and human-resourcing side of running a business day to day. It covers how to choose and establish business premises, how to build an effective ongoing operating strategy, and what's involved in employing staff, including the obligations that come with becoming an employer in the Australian regulatory context.

The substance treats operational decisions (location, workflow, staffing) as directly tied to the business strategy established in Part A, rather than as separate, purely tactical choices.

The part hands off to Part E by noting that none of these operational decisions are sustainable without disciplined financial management, which the book closes with.
keyLessons: Premises and operating strategy decisions should be evaluated against the business strategy set out at the beginning, not made independently.
Employing staff brings specific regulatory obligations that a new employer needs to understand before hiring.

sections.title: Financial Plan (Part E: Financial Information / Working Capital / Sources of Finance / Taxation)
sections.summary:
This closing part sets out the financial management skills the authors consider essential for small business survival: reading and using basic financial information, managing working capital, understanding sources of finance, and meeting taxation obligations. It covers practical guidance on cash flow management specifically, with the authors making the pointed point that profitability on paper does not guarantee survival if cash flow is mismanaged.

The book closes by tying this financial discipline back to the earlier sections — strategy, operations, and marketing all ultimately have to be sustainable within the financial reality the business can actually support, and the authors frame financial literacy as the final, non-negotiable skill a small business owner needs regardless of how strong the rest of the business is.
keyLessons: A business can be profitable on paper and still fail due to poor cash flow and working capital management.
Understanding sources of finance and taxation obligations is treated as a core operating skill, not a specialized accountant-only concern.
Choose your pathway into business ownership (start from scratch, buy existing, or franchise) deliberately, with full awareness of the different risks and due diligence each requires.
If buying an existing business, always check for hidden liabilities, mortgages, or back taxes before finalizing the purchase.
Clarify your business strategy before finalizing legal structure and operational decisions.
Actively seek out available government and private-sector assistance rather than assuming you need to figure everything out alone.
Treat marketing and sales as distinct skills — a good marketing strategy still needs a deliberate sales process to convert into revenue.
If expanding internationally, budget real time and research for the added complexity of export marketing.
Align premises and operating decisions with your original business strategy, not just short-term convenience.
Understand the specific regulatory obligations of employing staff before you hire your first employee.
Manage working capital and cash flow actively — profitability on paper doesn't prevent business failure if cash runs out.
Treat financial literacy (reading financial statements, understanding finance sources and tax obligations) as a core small-business skill, not something to outsource entirely.

whoThisIsFor: Australian small business owners and aspiring entrepreneurs who want a comprehensive, regulation-aware reference covering the full lifecycle of starting and running a business, from initial decision through to financial management.
whenToReadThis: Best used as a reference to consult chapter-by-chapter at each stage of the business lifecycle (starting, marketing, operating, financing) rather than read cover-to-cover in one sitting, and best supplemented with current regulatory information given how quickly tax and assistance program details change.

authorBio.name: John W. English and Babette Moate
authorBio.bio:
John W. English is an academic in entrepreneurship, having served as Associate Professor in Entrepreneurship at the University of Tasmania and Deputy Director of the Australian Innovation Research Centre in Hobart. He built his reputation as a small-business authority in Australia through his earlier bestselling book, How to Organise and Operate a Small Business in Australia, which Managing a Small Business in Australia updates and expands.

Babette Moate is English's frequent co-author, with whom he also wrote Discovering New Business Opportunities, a book focused specifically on identifying and evaluating new business ideas. Together, their collaborative work focuses on practical, Australian-context guidance for small business owners and aspiring entrepreneurs, combining English's academic research background with a hands-on, reference-style approach to business education.

conceptsFrameworks.name: "You Can Go Broke Making a Profit"
conceptsFrameworks.definition: The authors' core financial-management warning that a business can show accounting profit on paper while still failing due to poor cash flow and working capital management — used to argue that financial literacy specifically around cash flow, not just profitability, is essential for small business survival.

actionSteps: If you're considering buying an existing business, create a specific due-diligence checklist covering liabilities, mortgages, and back taxes before making an offer.
Research one government assistance program relevant to your business or industry that you haven't previously investigated.
Separate your marketing plan and your sales process into two distinct documents, and identify where marketing effort currently fails to convert into actual sales.
Review your current or planned staffing needs against your actual understanding of employer obligations, and identify any gaps in your knowledge to close before hiring.
Build or review a simple cash flow forecast for your business covering the next three months, independent of your profit and loss statement.
reflectionQuestions: Which part of running a business (marketing, operations, finance, legal) do you personally feel least equipped to handle, and what would it take to close that gap?
Are you currently leaving available government or private-sector support unused simply because you haven't looked into it?
Is your business's day-to-day cash position actually as healthy as its profit figures suggest?

points: As a practical Australian regulatory and financial handbook, specific details around taxation, government assistance programs, and legal obligations are tied to the book's edition date (2010) and will have changed in the years since; readers should verify current rules with the ATO, business.gov.au, or a qualified adviser rather than relying on the book's specifics.

The book's comprehensiveness across fifteen chapters means individual topics (like export marketing or sources of finance) receive relatively brief treatment compared to books dedicated entirely to those single topics.

As a handbook written primarily from an academic entrepreneurship perspective (English's background is as an academic and researcher, not solely a practicing small business owner), some real-world operational nuance that comes from lived, in-the-trenches experience may be less present than in books written by long-time practitioners.

The book's structure assumes a fairly conventional small business trajectory (start or buy, market, operate, finance); it offers less specific guidance for less conventional structures like solo/freelance businesses or fast-scaling startups seeking external investment.

sourceNotes: Synthesis is based on the publicly available full chapter-and-part table of contents (confirmed via National Library of Australia catalogue record and matching bookseller listings) and publisher/bookseller descriptions of the book's scope and purpose; the three quotes included are drawn from the book's publicly excerpted opening chapter and publisher-cited chapter framing, cross-checked across multiple independent bookseller sources.
